evidence: On March 5, 2025, the Texas A&M Queer Empowerment Council, a recognized student organization, filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas against the Texas A&M Board of Regents and university officials.
The lawsuit challenged the Board of Regents' February 28, 2025 resolution banning drag shows from campus 'Special Event Venues.'
The student organization had been hosting an annual drag show called 'Draggieland' at the campus Rudder Theatre since 2020, with the 2025 performance scheduled for March 27.
The show was fully funded by the student group, not the university, and featured performers in a pageant-style format discussing what drag means to them.
Past performances had sold out the 750-seat theater.

The Board's resolution stated that drag shows were inconsistent with the university's values because they 'demean women' and involve 'mockery or objectification of women,' potentially creating a hostile environment under Title IX.

The Board also cited President Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order on 'Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism' as justification, arguing that allowing drag shows might violate federal funding restrictions.
The student organization brought claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 and 1988 and the Declaratory Judgment Act, alleging violations of the First and Fourteenth Amendments.
They argued the ban constituted impermissible viewpoint discrimination and a prior restraint on speech.
The complaint also included a claim under the Texas Open Meetings Act, alleging the Board provided inadequate public notice for its February 28 meeting.
After expedited briefing and a hearing on March 18, 2025, Judge Rosenthal granted the preliminary injunction on March 24, 2025.
The court found that drag shows are protected expressive conduct under the First Amendment and that the Board's ban constituted impermissible viewpoint discrimination.
The preliminary injunction allowed Draggieland to proceed as scheduled on March 27, 2025, without requiring the student organization to post a bond.
The defendants filed a notice of appeal to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals on March 28, 2025 (case no. 25-20108), along with a motion to stay the preliminary injunction pending appeal.
The case remains active with ongoing proceedings regarding the stay motion and the underlying constitutional claims.
The student organization was represented by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE).
The case was assigned to Senior U.S. District Judge Lee H. Rosenthal.

The Board's resolution claims drag shows demean women and involve mockery or objectification of women, potentially creating a hostile environment under Title IX, and cites President Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order on 'Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism' as justification. evidence: Between April 4-8, 2025, ICE's Student and Exchange Visitor Program terminated the SEVIS records of hundreds of F-1 visa holders nationwide, including all five plaintiffs. The terminations cited 'Otherwise Failing to Maintain Status – Individual identified in criminal records check and/or has had their visa revoked' as the reason.

On April 11, 2025, five international students proceeding under pseudonyms filed suit in the Northern District of California challenging the unlawful termination of their Student and Exchange Visitor Information Systems (SEVIS) records by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The students alleged that their minor criminal histories—which included a misdemeanor DUI conviction, a dismissed disturbing the peace charge, dismissed criminal charges, and arrests without charges—did not meet the regulatory standards for status termination under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1.

The students brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging the SEVIS terminations were unauthorized, arbitrary and capricious, and violated procedural due process. They also asserted Fifth Amendment due process violations.
They sought declaratory relief finding the terminations unlawful, restoration of their SEVIS records, and injunctive relief preventing enforcement actions, detention, and removal.

On April 16, 2025, the students filed a motion for a temporary restraining order. Judge Wise granted the TRO on April 17, 2025, enjoining defendants from arresting, detaining, or transferring the students and from imposing legal effects based on the SEVIS terminations.
On May 22, 2025, Judge White granted the motion for preliminary injunction.
The government filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on July 21, 2025 (Case No. 25-4523), and subsequently moved to stay the injunction pending appeal in August 2025.
The case was related to multiple similar cases involving international students facing SEVIS terminations under comparable circumstances.

evidence: This case was filed on April 7, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia before Judge Irene C. Berger. Harry Wiley, a coal miner, brought this class action lawsuit on behalf of himself and all coal miners with evidence of pneumoconiosis (black lung disease) against Robert F. Kennedy Jr., in his official capacity as Secretary of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

The case arises from defendants' decision to effectively shut down the Coal Workers' Health Surveillance Program (CWHSP) and related "Part 90" job transfer program operated by the Respiratory Health Division within the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) in Morgantown, West Virginia. These programs, mandated by the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act and Mine Safety and Health Act (30 U.S.C. § 843), provide medical screening for coal miners and the right to transfer to low-dust jobs when they develop black lung disease. On April 1, 2025, defendants terminated or placed on administrative leave nearly all employees in the Respiratory Health Division, including the chief medical officer, effectively shuttering these critical health and safety programs.

The plaintiff Harry Wiley is a coal miner with 38 years of experience who was diagnosed with black lung disease in November 2024. He submitted an application for Part 90 job transfer rights to NIOSH in November 2024 but received no response due to the program closure. Black lung is a progressive, incurable disease that worsens with continued dust exposure, making early intervention and job transfers critical to prevent debilitating progression.

On April 21, 2025, plaintiff filed a motion for preliminary injunction. After a hearing on May 7, 2025, that included testimony from NIOSH employees and affected miners, Judge Berger granted the preliminary injunction on May 13, 2025. The court found that plaintiff demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm from continued dust exposure without access to job transfer rights, and that the public interest favored maintaining the congressionally mandated programs. The court ordered that the reduction-in-force notices be enjoined and rescinded to facilitate full restoration of the NIOSH Respiratory Health Division, and that there be no gap in the protections and services mandated by Congress. Defendants were required to submit written certification of compliance within 20 days.

The court rejected defendants' arguments that the case involved non-reviewable personnel decisions, finding instead that plaintiff challenged the elimination of statutorily required programs, not employment actions per se. The court also found that the program closure constituted final agency action subject to review under the APA, despite defendants' arguments that their reorganization was still in progress.

On July 9, 2025, plaintiff moved for leave to file a second amended complaint, which was granted on August 14, 2025. The case remains active with trial scheduled for May 4, 2026. The preliminary injunction requires defendants to maintain the coal miner health surveillance and job transfer programs during the pendency of the litigation.

evidence: This case was filed on April 20, 2023, by parents Ashley Willey and Sean Willey against Sweetwater County School District #1's Board of Trustees and four individual defendants: Superintendent Kelly McGovern, Assistant Superintendent Nicole Bolton, Director of Student Services Kayci Arnoldi, and Principal Bryant Blake.

The parents' daughter, A.S., was a 16-year-old student at Black Butte High School who had a history of childhood trauma and was receiving treatment for ADHD, PTSD, and symptoms of gender dysphoria from a private counselor chosen by her parents.
During the 2021-2022 school year, A.S. told school staff she wanted to be treated as a boy, use the male name "C" and male pronouns, and requested that this information be concealed from her parents.

Pursuant to district policy, school personnel agreed to this arrangement and for over six months treated A.S. as a boy at school while using her legal name and female pronouns when communicating with her parents.
The parents only discovered this deception in March 2022 when Mrs. Willey happened to meet teachers at a district training who inadvertently revealed the situation.

The district had implemented what the parents termed "the Policy," consisting of two components: a "Preferred Names Policy" requiring staff to use students' preferred names and pronouns even if they differ from biological sex, and a "Parent Concealment Policy" requiring staff to conceal this information from parents unless the student consents.
Mrs. Willey, who was also employed as a teacher by the district, was told she must comply with the Policy despite her religious objections and was denied accommodations for her religious beliefs.

The parents brought claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging violations of their Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process rights to direct their children's upbringing and make mental health decisions, and Mrs. Willey's First Amendment rights to free exercise of religion and free speech.
They sought declaratory and injunctive relief as well as monetary damages.
On April 21, 2023, the parents filed a motion for preliminary injunction.

Judge Scott W. Skavdahl granted the motion in part on June 30, 2023, enjoining the district from precluding employees from responding to parental inquiries about students' preferred names or pronouns and from requiring employees to lie to parents about such requests, but denied the injunction as to other aspects of the policy.

On April 28, 2025, Judge Skavdahl granted summary judgment in favor of the defendants on all remaining claims and dismissed Sean Willey from the action, leaving Ashley Willey as the sole remaining plaintiff before dismissing all her claims as well.
The plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal on May 23, 2025, appealing to the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals under case number 25-8027.

The parents claim the policy violated their Fourteenth Amendment due-process rights to direct their children's upbringing and mental-health decisions, as well as Mrs. Willey's First Amendment free-exercise and free-speech rights. The parents sought declaratory and injunctive relief and monetary damages. The case progressed through motions, a preliminary injunction, summary judgment, and an appeal to the Tenth Circuit.

evidence: This class action lawsuit was filed on May 10, 2016, by over thirty current and former residents of the Alexander County Housing Authority (ACHA) against ACHA, Executive Director James Wilson, and Finance Director Martha Franklin.

The plaintiffs alleged that ACHA engaged in racial and familial status discrimination at its McBride and Elmwood family housing developments in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Illinois Civil Rights Act of 2003.
According to the complaint, approximately 97% of residents in McBride and Elmwood were African-American, while white households predominated in other ACHA developments like Connell Smith.

The plaintiffs claimed this segregation was intentional and echoed discriminatory practices from decades earlier—the U.S. Department of Justice had sued ACHA in 1974 for intentionally segregating these same housing complexes by race, resulting in a settlement agreement.
Plaintiffs described units infested with mice, roaches, and bedbugs; serious mold problems; broken plumbing, heating, and electrical systems; and security issues.
Meanwhile, ACHA allegedly maintained the Connell Smith development in satisfactory condition and provided security cameras and guards.
HUD's 2014 finding that ACHA had violated Title VI through intentional racial segregation was referenced as supporting evidence.

The complaint also alleged that ACHA improperly prohibited families with children from living in certain developments like Connell Smith and Shoemaker, which did not qualify as senior housing under federal law.

evidence: The United States filed this civil rights enforcement action against the South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice on April 14, 2022, under the pattern or practice provision of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, 34 U.S.C. § 12601.
The case was resolved through a comprehensive settlement agreement signed by the parties on April 13, 2022, the day before the complaint was filed.
The lawsuit arose from a DOJ investigation that began in 2017 examining conditions at the Broad River Road Complex (BRRC), South Carolina's long-term juvenile commitment facility.
The facility houses youth aged 17 and younger who have been adjudicated delinquent, with an average daily population of over 100 youth and average stays of six to seven months.
The investigation involved multiple site visits, staff and youth interviews, document review, and video analysis.
Specifically, between July 2018 and May 2019, there were 134 fights and 71 assaults resulting in 99 injuries to youth, with violence occurring on average two out of every three days.
Staff engaged in dangerous tactics including choking, punching, kicking, and twisting youth's arms, often in response to verbal non-compliance rather than physical threats.
Youth were placed in isolation for minor infractions like profanity or disrespect, sometimes for weeks or months in small, dark cells for 23 hours daily without meaningful education or programming.

DOJ issued two findings reports documenting constitutional violations. The February 5, 2020 report concluded that the Department of Juvenile Justice failed to keep youth reasonably safe from youth-on-youth violence and subjected youth to prolonged, punitive isolation in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause. The April 14, 2022 report found that staff used excessive force against youth.

The agreement addresses staffing levels, physical plant security, use of force policies, isolation practices, staff training, investigation procedures, and quality assurance systems. Key provisions include conducting a staffing study, eliminating blind spots through improved surveillance, implementing positive behavior management programs, restricting use of force to situations involving immediate danger, limiting isolation to four hours except with supervisory approval, providing meaningful education during any isolation, and establishing a multidisciplinary team to review isolation placements.

The settlement includes extensive monitoring through a Subject Matter Expert to be jointly selected by the parties, with a budget not exceeding $225,000 in the first year. The expert will conduct semi-annual compliance assessments and provide technical assistance.

On April 14, 2022, the parties filed a joint motion for conditional dismissal, which Judge Lewis granted on April 20, 2022. The court dismissed the case without prejudice while retaining jurisdiction to resolve any disputes over compliance with the settlement agreement. The judgment was entered the same day, with the case remaining subject to potential reinstatement if material breach occurs.

evidence: On May 21, 2025, a federal grand jury in the Middle District of Tennessee indicted Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia on two counts related to human smuggling: conspiracy to unlawfully transport illegal aliens for financial gain and illegal transportation of illegal aliens for financial gain, both in violation of 8 U.S.C. § 1324.

The charges stem from a November 30, 2022 traffic stop by Tennessee Highway Patrol, during which Abrego was allegedly driving a vehicle containing nine individuals who were being transported illegally for financial compensation.

The government's evidence includes testimony from cooperating witnesses who claim Abrego participated in a broader human smuggling conspiracy operated by a business called 'Trans Express,' phone records showing communications with the conspiracy's leader during the traffic stop, and a roster allegedly showing that one of the transported individuals was a minor.
The government argued that Abrego transported approximately 120 undocumented individuals and was paid $1,000-$1,500 per trip.
He had been living in the United States for over a decade with his family and had an immigration court order granting withholding of removal to El Salvador.
However, he was removed to El Salvador in March 2025.

A federal court in Maryland ordered his return, leading to the Supreme Court case Noem v. Abrego Garcia, 145 S. Ct. 1017 (2025), which affirmed that the government must facilitate his return from El Salvador.
He was arrested upon his return to the United States on June 6, 2025.

evidence: On July 1, 2025, the City of Columbus, Ohio; the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, Maryland; the City of Chicago, Illinois; Doctors for America; and Main Street Alliance filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland challenging federal regulations under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The plaintiffs, represented by private counsel from the Democracy Forward Foundation, sought declaratory and injunctive relief against Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. as Secretary of Health and Human Services, the Department of Health and Human Services, Mehmet Oz as Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, and CMS itself.
The lawsuit challenges the "Marketplace Integrity and Affordability Rule", a regulation published by CMS on June 25, 2025, and scheduled to take effect on August 25, 2025.

According to the complaint, the rule will cause at least 1.8 million Americans to lose coverage on ACA health insurance exchanges in 2026 and result in higher premiums and out-of-pocket costs for remaining enrollees.

The challenged rule includes several key provisions: a $5 monthly surcharge on certain low-income enrollees until they confirm eligibility; changes to premium adjustment methodology that increase cost-sharing limits; expansion of allowable variation in actuarial value calculations; allowing insurers to deny coverage to individuals with past-due premiums; enhanced verification requirements for special enrollment periods; reinstating a failure-to-reconcile penalty for tax credit recipients; and stricter income verification requirements when applicant data doesn't match IRS records.

Plaintiffs alleged these provisions are both contrary to law and arbitrary and capricious under the APA. They argued the rule violates the ACA's guaranteed-issue requirement, exceeds CMS's statutory authority regarding tax credit calculations, and lacks adequate justification for burdens imposed on consumers.

The city plaintiffs claimed standing based on anticipated increased costs for uncompensated care as more residents become uninsured, while Main Street Alliance asserted associational standing on behalf of small business members who rely on ACA marketplace coverage.

On July 2, 2025, plaintiffs filed a motion for a stay under 5 U.S.C. § 705 or preliminary injunction. After briefing and a hearing on August 14, 2025, Judge Hurson issued a memorandum opinion on August 22, 2025, granting the motion in part and denying it in part.
The court found plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits regarding seven provisions of the rule but not on two others.

The court concluded that plaintiffs would suffer irreparable harm without relief, as the City Plaintiffs would face increased uncompensated care costs not recoverable due to sovereign immunity, and at least one Main Street Alliance member might be forced to close her business due to unaffordable insurance premium increases.

The court stayed seven provisions of the rule pending final resolution of the case: the $5 premium penalty, revocation of guaranteed coverage for past-due premiums, the failure-to-reconcile policy, special enrollment period verification requirements, income verification requirements when projected income differs from trusted sources, changes to actuarial value de minimis ranges, and changes to self-attestation policy when tax data is unavailable.
However, the court declined to stay provisions regarding premium adjustment percentage methodology and elimination of automatic 60-day extensions for resolving income inconsistencies.
The court issued a clarifying order on August 25, 2025, specifying exactly which regulatory provisions were stayed.

The plaintiffs allege the rule will cause at least 1.8 million Americans to lose ACA coverage in 2026 and increase premiums and out‑of‑pocket costs, and that its provisions—including a $5 monthly surcharge, changes to premium adjustment methodology, actuarial value variations, denial of coverage for past‑due premiums, enhanced special enrollment verification, a failure‑to‑reconcile penalty, and stricter income verification—are contrary to law, violate the ACA's guaranteed‑issue requirement, exceed CMS's statutory authority, and impose unjustified burdens. They assert standing based on anticipated uncompensated care costs and associational interest of small businesses. A motion for stay was filed on July 2, 2025, and Judge Hurson granted a partial stay on August 22, 2025, staying seven provisions and leaving two others in effect. The court concluded plaintiffs would suffer irreparable harm and clarified the stayed provisions in an order on August 25, 2025.

evidence: On May 27, 2025, National Public Radio (NPR) and three local public radio stations—Aspen Public Radio, Colorado Public Radio, and KSUT Public Radio—filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against President Donald Trump and various federal officials and agencies.
The case, assigned to Judge Randolph D. Moss, challenges Executive Order 14290, titled "Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media," which President Trump issued on May 1, 2025.

The Executive Order directed CPB and federal agencies to terminate all direct and indirect funding to NPR and the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), stating that these organizations do not "present a fair, accurate, or unbiased portrayal of current events."

The plaintiffs' legal challenge rests on both constitutional and statutory grounds. They argue the Order violates the First Amendment's guarantees of freedom of speech, press, and association by engaging in viewpoint-based discrimination and retaliation against NPR for its protected journalistic activities. They also claim Fifth Amendment due process violations for denying funding without adequate notice or process.

On June 13, 2025, the plaintiffs moved for summary judgment, seeking declaratory relief that the Executive Order is unlawful and permanent injunctive relief preventing its implementation. The federal defendants filed a cross-motion for summary judgment on July 12, 2025, arguing that the plaintiffs lack a viable cause of action, their claims are not ripe for review, and the Order does not violate the Constitution or federal statutes when the government chooses not to subsidize particular speech.
The case also attracted significant amicus support, with briefs filed by news organizations, civil liberties groups, and 23 states supporting the plaintiffs' position.
The factual backdrop includes the Administration's efforts to replace non-compliant CPB board members and statements by President Trump criticizing NPR's coverage dating back to his first term.

evidence: On April 3, 2025, six major federal employee unions filed suit challenging Executive Order 14251, which President Trump issued on March 27, 2025.

Executive Order 14251 excluded over 40 federal departments, agencies, and subdivisions from coverage under the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute (Chapter 71 of Title 5), effectively eliminating collective bargaining rights for approximately two-thirds of the federal workforce.

The order was issued under Section 7103(b)(1) of the statute, which permits presidential exclusions when agencies have primary national security functions and collective bargaining cannot be applied consistent with national security requirements.

"Accompanying the executive order, the White House issued a Fact Sheet that criticized 'hostile Federal unions' who 'declared war on President Trump's agenda' and were "'fighting back'" against Trump.'."

The Office of Personnel Management simultaneously issued guidance instructing affected agencies to terminate collective bargaining agreements, cease grievance procedures, end payroll deduction of union dues, and reassign employees conducting union business on official time.

The unions alleged violations of their First Amendment rights through retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, claiming the order was issued in response to their protected speech activities, including filing lawsuits against Trump administration policies and making public statements critical of the administration.

They also alleged the order was ultra vires, exceeding the President's authority under Chapter 71, and violated Fifth Amendment procedural due process, property rights in existing collective bargaining agreements, and equal protection principles.
On April 7, 2025, plaintiffs filed an ex parte motion for a temporary restraining order, which the court treated as a preliminary injunction motion.
On June 24, 2025, Judge Donato granted the preliminary injunction, finding plaintiffs raised serious First Amendment questions warranting preservation of the status quo pending trial.
The preliminary injunction enjoined defendants from implementing Section 2 of Executive Order 14251 against plaintiffs and their members, and required plaintiffs to post a $60,000 bond.
The government immediately appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on June 26, 2025, and filed an emergency motion to stay the injunction pending appeal.
The district court denied the stay motion on July 8, 2025.
However, the Ninth Circuit granted an administrative stay on July 10, 2025, and on August 1, 2025, issued a full stay of the preliminary injunction pending appeal.
The case involves numerous related federal court challenges to Executive Order 14251 filed by other unions and federal employees across multiple jurisdictions.
The appellate proceedings have effectively suspended the preliminary injunction while the underlying constitutional and statutory claims await further litigation on the merits.
The unions sought declaratory and injunctive relief and attorney's fees.
extracted.value: The case involves six federal employee unions filing suit on April 3, 2025, challenging President Trump's Executive Order 14251 issued on March 27, 2025, which excluded over 40 federal departments from collective bargaining rights; the plaintiffs allege First Amendment retaliation, ultra vires, and Fifth Amendment violations, and the court granted a preliminary injunction on June 24, 2025, but the Ninth Circuit stayed the injunction pending appeal; the case is grounded in Section 7103(b)(1) of the statute and the White House Fact Sheet and OPM guidance that accompanied the order, and it is part of a broader set of federal court challenges to the order.

The case arose from the Department of Education's termination of the school district's $6 million mental health grant, which was part of the $1 billion Bipartisan Safer Communities Act passed by Congress in 2022 following the Uvalde school shooting.

The grant termination occurred after the Trump Administration issued several executive orders targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs, including Executive Order No. 14151 ("Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing"), Executive Order No. 14173 ("Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity"), and Executive Order No. 14190 ("Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling").
On February 14, 2025, the Department issued a Dear Colleague Letter threatening schools with loss of federal funding if they continued pursuing ambiguously defined "DEI programs."

On April 29, 2025, the Department terminated the school district's grant through a "Notice of Non-Continuation of Grant Award," determining that the mental health programs violated federal civil rights law, conflicted with the Department's policy of prioritizing merit and excellence, undermined student well-being, or constituted inappropriate use of federal funds.
The school district had received $3,605,500 through December 2025 and was entitled to an additional $2,394,500 through 2027.

The school district had received this five-year grant and had been using the funds to hire mental health professionals, establish wellness rooms, and provide comprehensive mental health services to approximately 2,500 students.

The evidence showed that the grant had allowed the district to hire seven additional mental health professionals, establish wellness rooms used by 830 students (40% of total enrollment), reduce bullying reports by 30%, and decrease disruptive behavior incidents significantly.
On July 18, 2025, Judge Johnson denied the motion for preliminary injunction and dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of jurisdiction.

The court relied heavily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Department of Education v. California, which found that district courts lack jurisdiction to order payment of money under the APA when the core issue involves contract enforcement.

The case highlighted the ongoing legal battles over the Trump Administration's efforts to eliminate DEI-related federal funding and raised important questions about the scope of federal court jurisdiction over government contract disputes framed as constitutional challenges.

The court found that despite the school district's attempt to frame the case as constitutional and administrative law claims, the essence of the lawsuit was a contract dispute seeking payment of grant money from the federal government. Under the Tucker Act, such claims must be brought in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, not federal district court.
The school district filed a motion for temporary restraining order and/or preliminary injunction on June 23, 2025.

evidence: On March 31, 2025, three groups of plaintiffs filed consolidated lawsuits challenging President Donald Trump's Executive Order 14,248, "Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections," issued March 25, 2025.
The nonpartisan plaintiffs included civil rights organizations like the League of United Latin American Citizens, League of Women Voters entities, NAACP, and student organizations.
The Democratic Party plaintiffs included the Democratic National Committee, related campaign committees, and congressional leaders Charles Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries.
The case was assigned to Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The Executive Order directed several federal agencies to take actions regarding voter registration and election administration. Section 2(a) ordered the Election Assistance Commission to require documentary proof of citizenship on the federal voter registration form within 30 days. Section 2(b) directed the Department of Homeland Security and State Department to share citizenship databases with states and the U.S. DOGE Service to identify unqualified voters. Section 2(d) instructed federal agencies serving as voter registration agencies to assess citizenship before providing registration forms to public assistance recipients. Section 7(a) directed the Attorney General to enforce federal Election Day statutes against states that count mail ballots received after Election Day. Section 7(b) ordered the EAC to withhold federal election funding from states that don't impose Election Day ballot receipt deadlines.

Plaintiffs brought ultra vires challenges arguing the President lacks constitutional authority to regulate federal elections, which the Constitution reserves to states and Congress under the Elections Clause. They also raised claims under the National Voter Registration Act, Help America Vote Act, and Privacy Act. Plaintiffs sought declaratory and injunctive relief, represented by various civil rights organizations, legal services groups, and political party counsel.

On April 7, 2025, both the nonpartisan and Democratic Party plaintiffs filed separate motions for preliminary injunctions. The Republican National Committee intervened as a defendant. After a hearing on April 17, 2025, Judge Kollar-Kotelly issued a preliminary injunction on April 24, 2025, granting relief in part.

The court enjoined implementation of Section 2(a), finding the President lacks authority to unilaterally direct the independent, bipartisan EAC to alter the federal voter registration form, which Congress assigned to the EAC through specific notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures under the NVRA and HAVA. The court also enjoined Section 2(d), ruling it violated the NVRA's mandatory requirement that voter registration agencies provide registration forms to all service applicants unless they decline in writing.

However, the court denied preliminary relief on Sections 2(b), 7(a), and 7(b). For Section 2(b), the court found the challenge premature since the Executive Order contained saving clauses requiring compliance with applicable law, and agencies had not yet taken concrete action that would violate the Privacy Act. For Section 7(a), the court determined the Democratic Party plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge enforcement actions directed at states, not the plaintiffs themselves. For Section 7(b), the court found plaintiffs had not established the substantial likelihood of standing required for preliminary relief, as their claimed injuries from potential state responses to funding threats were too speculative.

The court's central reasoning rested on separation of powers principles. Under the Constitution's Elections Clause, states have initial authority to regulate federal elections, subject only to Congressional oversight—the President has no role. The Framers deliberately excluded presidential authority over elections, as evidenced in the Federalist Papers.

Congress exercised its Elections Clause power through the NVRA and HAVA, creating specific procedures for the independent EAC to maintain election forms through bipartisan consensus and notice-and-comment rulemaking.
The President cannot circumvent these congressional mandates through executive orders.

The court found plaintiffs had standing through organizational injury (interference with core voter registration activities) and associational standing on behalf of members whose voting rights would be burdened.

The court noted irreparable harm given the upcoming Arizona special congressional election with a June 16, 2025 voter registration deadline, emphasizing that election-related injuries cannot be remedied after deadlines pass.
The court applied the Purcell principle but found it supported rather than barred relief, since the injunction preserved the existing status quo against the Executive Order's changes.

The preliminary injunctions run against the EAC and its commissioners regarding Section 2(a), and against federal departments serving as voter registration agencies (Defense, Veterans Affairs, Interior, Small Business Administration) and their secretaries regarding Section 2(d). The court declined to require an injunction bond.
The case remains pending on the merits, with summary judgment motions filed by August 2025.

evidence: This case was filed on April 28, 2025, in the Western District of Washington before Judge Ricardo S. Martinez by six plaintiff organizations challenging federal defendants' actions to dismantle the Head Start program.

First, defendants implemented sweeping bans on activities that "promote" or "advance" "diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility" (DEIA) through a March 14, 2025 letter and an April 16, 2025 certification requirement incorporated into grant awards.

Second, defendants conducted mass layoffs eliminating 60% of Office of Head Start staff and closing half of the regional offices on April 1, 2025, leaving 23 states without Head Start program support.

Plaintiffs allege these actions create an impossible double-bind for Head Start agencies, which must either comply with the vague DEIA ban (risking violation of statutory obligations to serve diverse populations) or face loss of federal funding covering 80% of program costs.

The Head Start Act specifically requires agencies to meet "diverse needs" of communities, provide culturally and linguistically appropriate services, serve children with disabilities inclusively, and recruit diverse staff—all potentially prohibited under the DEIA ban.
The case includes extensive declarations from Head Start administrators and parents documenting operational disruptions, program closures, and harms to families served by Head Start programs.

After a hearing on August 5, 2025, the court issued an order on August 8, 2025, noting that defendants stipulated to certain relief making the TRO motion moot, but converted it to a preliminary injunction motion with a hearing scheduled for September 9, 2025.
The court granted plaintiffs' motion to file declarations under pseudonym on June 16, 2025, and motion to amend the complaint on August 19, 2025, with a second amended complaint filed the same day.

These actions are supported by the letters and certification, the layoff and closure records, and declarations from administrators and parents documenting operational disruptions and harms. Background information includes the Head Start Act’s obligations to serve diverse populations, the federal funding structure (80 % federal), and the plaintiffs’ claim that the DEIA ban creates an impossible double‑bind for agencies.

evidence: On March 25, 2025, the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and American Federation of Teachers (AFT), both labor unions representing faculty and academic professionals, filed suit in the Southern District of New York against multiple federal executive agencies and officials, seeking to restore approximately $400 million in terminated federal grants and contracts to Columbia University. Judge Mary Kay Vyskocil presided over the case.

The case arose from escalating tensions at Columbia University following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, which led to widespread campus protests and reports of antisemitic incidents. According to Columbia's own task force reports, Jewish students faced harassment, threats, and physical assaults, particularly during the spring 2024 occupation of Hamilton Hall and establishment of protest encampments that Columbia allowed to remain for months.
On January 29, 2025, shortly after taking office, President Trump issued an Executive Order directing agencies to combat antisemitism using "all available appropriate legal tools."

On February 3, 2025, the Department of Justice announced formation of a multi‑agency Task Force to Combat Anti‑Semitism led by Leo Terrell, and the Department of Education announced Title VI investigations into Columbia and four other universities.

After warning Columbia on March 3, 2025 that the government was reviewing its federal funding relationships, the agencies announced on March 7, 2025 the "immediate cancellation of approximately $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University due to the school's continued inaction in the face of persistent harassment of Jewish students."

On March 13, 2025, the agencies sent Columbia a letter listing nine demands as "preconditions for formal negotiations regarding Columbia University's continued financial relationship with the United States government," including enforcing disciplinary policies with "expulsion or multi‑year suspension," abolishing Columbia's University Judicial Board, implementing mask bans, placing the Middle East, South Asian, and African Studies (MESAAS) department under "academic receivership for a minimum of five years," and reforming admissions practices.

Columbia responded on March 21, 2025 by announcing eighteen actions, many of which aligned with but differed from the government's demands. Notably, evidence showed Columbia had been planning these reforms for months before receiving any government demands.

The defendants maintained they terminated funding not under Title VI procedures, but because the grants and contracts "no longer effectuate . . . agency priorities" and "for the convenience of the Government" under standard grant termination provisions in 2 C.F.R. § 200.340(a)(4) and Federal Acquisition Regulation clauses. The National Institutes of Health terminated over 400 grants totaling more than $250 million, while the Departments of Education and Health & Human Services terminated additional grants and contracts.

Plaintiffs' complaint asserted ten claims under the First Amendment (free speech and academic freedom violations), Administrative Procedure Act (procedural and substantive violations), separation of powers/ultra vires theories, Fifth Amendment Due Process, Tenth Amendment/Spending Clause, and the "unconstitutional conditions" doctrine. They argued defendants violated Title VI's procedural requirements for funding termination and unconstitutionally coerced Columbia to suppress speech and academic freedom.

On June 16, 2025, Judge Vyskocil denied the preliminary injunction motion and dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of standing. The court found plaintiffs could not demonstrate Article III standing because: (1) neither plaintiffs nor their members were parties to the grants and contracts, which were awarded to Columbia University; (2) any alleged speech chilling by plaintiffs' members was speculative and not fairly traceable to defendants' actions, since Columbia had independently planned its reforms months before any government demands; (3) plaintiffs could not establish organizational standing by spending money to oppose defendants' actions; and (4) Columbia had provided salary coverage to affected personnel, mitigating any economic harm.

The court was notably critical of plaintiffs' legal theories, observing that Title VI covers only race, color, and national origin—not religion—making it unlikely to be the exclusive vehicle for combating antisemitism. The court also referenced the Supreme Court's recent decision in Department of Education v. California, which suggested that grant termination claims sound in contract and belong in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act rather than in district court under the APA.

Plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal to the Second Circuit on June 16, 2025. The related case Khalil v. Trustees of Columbia University, where Columbia students sought similar relief, was also denied for lack of standing. Notably, Columbia University itself was not a party to this litigation, appearing only in a limited capacity to oppose disclosure of internal communications, and stating it was 'actively engaged in negotiations with Defendants about the terminated awards.'

evidence: On May 7, 2025, sixteen states and the District of Columbia filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington against the U.S. Department of Transportation, Secretary Sean Duffy, the Federal Highway Administration, and Acting Administrator Gloria M. Shepherd, represented by their respective state attorneys general. The case is assigned to Judge Tana Lin.

The lawsuit challenges defendants' suspension of the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program, a $5 billion initiative established by Congress in the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to fund electric vehicle charging infrastructure across the country. Under the statute, funds must be distributed to states according to a mandatory formula, with states required to submit deployment plans describing how they will use the funds for EV charging infrastructure.

The dispute arose from President Trump's January 20, 2025 "Unleashing American Energy" executive order directing all federal agencies to "immediately pause the disbursement of funds" from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, including NEVI Formula Program funds. On February 6, 2025, FHWA sent states a letter rescinding all NEVI Formula Program guidance, revoking all previously approved state deployment plans, and prohibiting new fund obligations until updated guidance could be issued. This action effectively froze approximately $2.74 billion in available funds.

Plaintiffs brought six causes of action: three Administrative Procedure Act violations (excess of statutory authority, arbitrary and capricious agency action, and failure to follow required procedures), violation of the separation of powers doctrine, violation of the Take Care Clause, and common law ultra vires. They sought declaratory and injunctive relief to restore the program and prevent unlawful withholding of congressionally appropriated funds.

The states argued that defendants lacked authority under the IIJA to categorically suspend the program, and that the statute provides only limited circumstances under which funds may be withheld, requiring specific procedural safeguards that were not followed. They alleged immediate harm from disrupted infrastructure projects, cancelled solicitations, lost partnerships, and administrative burdens.

On June 17, 2025, the court held oral argument on plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction. Seven public interest organizations, including Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council, successfully moved to intervene as party plaintiffs, with the court granting their intervention motion on July 23, 2025.

On June 24, 2025, Judge Tana Lin issued an order granting the preliminary injunction in part and denying it in part. The court found that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits of their APA and constitutional claims, concluding that defendants had exceeded their statutory authority and violated the separation of powers doctrine. The injunction was granted for fourteen plaintiff states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, and Wisconsin) but denied for the District of Columbia, Minnesota, and Vermont due to insufficient evidence of irreparable harm.

The preliminary injunction, effective July 2, 2025, enjoins defendants from suspending or revoking previously-approved state deployment plans and from withholding NEVI Formula Program funds except as permitted by the IIJA's specific procedures. The injunction restores the affected states' deployment plans to their legal status prior to the February 6, 2025 FHWA letter and requires defendants to process authorization requests for specific EV charging infrastructure projects. The court waived any bond requirement and the preliminary injunction remains in effect pending further court orders.
The case involves ongoing discovery and dispositive motion practice, with cross-motions for summary judgment scheduled for briefing through October 2025.

evidence: This case was filed on March 13, 2025, in the Southern District of New York before Judge Arun Subramanian.

Eight students at Columbia University and Barnard College, proceeding under pseudonyms, sued Columbia University and its trustees, the House Committee on Education and Workforce and its Chairman Tim Walberg, and various federal agency officials involved in a Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism.
The case arises from a congressional investigation into antisemitism on college campuses that began in 2024.

On February 13, 2025, the Committee sent a letter requesting disciplinary records relating to eleven specific incidents involving student activism, which the plaintiffs claim would encompass records of hundreds of students.
Simultaneously, federal agencies including the Department of Education, Department of Health and Human Services, and General Services Administration threatened Columbia with loss of federal funding.
On March 7, 2025, the Trump administration announced it had canceled approximately $400 million in federal grants to Columbia.

On March 13, 2025, these agencies sent Columbia a letter demanding compliance with specific policy changes as a 'precondition for formal negotiations regarding Columbia University's continued financial relationship with the United States government.'

The demands included harsh disciplinary measures against students involved in protests, elimination of the University Judicial Board, a campus mask ban, increased law enforcement presence, placing the Middle East, South Asian, and African Studies department under 'academic receivership,' and adoption of a specific definition of antisemitism.

The plaintiffs allege this constitutes illegal 'jawboning' - government officials using threats and coercion against a private intermediary (Columbia) to suppress speech and association rights the government cannot directly restrict.

They claim violations of the First Amendment's Free Speech and Association Clauses, breach of contract based on Columbia's promises of academic freedom, and violations of Title VI procedures and the Administrative Procedure Act.
The plaintiffs seek declaratory judgment, permanent injunctive relief preventing further record disclosures and compliance with federal demands, and monetary damages for records already produced.
On March 19, 2025, the plaintiffs filed a motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, which the Court denied without prejudice on April 4, 2025.
The Court also ordered that Columbia must provide thirty days' notice before furnishing any student records or identifying information to Congress.

Defendants filed motions to dismiss on May 23, 2025, arguing various jurisdictional and substantive defenses including Speech or Debate Clause immunity, sovereign immunity, lack of standing, and failure to state a claim.
Briefing on the motions to dismiss and a renewed motion for preliminary injunction is ongoing.
The Court noted that the Speech or Debate Clause bars relief against the Congressional defendants, but granted plaintiffs leave to file an amended complaint.
The plaintiffs are represented by private counsel from multiple organizations including Dratel & Lewis and CAIR Legal Defense Fund.

evidence: On May 5, 2025, nineteen states and the District of Columbia filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island against HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and various HHS agencies, challenging the agency's planned mass workforce reduction and reorganization.
The case was assigned to District Judge Melissa R. DuBose, with state attorneys general representing the plaintiffs.

The lawsuit arose from HHS's March 27, 2025 announcement titled "HHS Announces Transformation to Make America Healthy Again" (the "March 27 Communiqué"), which outlined plans to terminate 10,000 full-time employees, consolidate 28 divisions into 15, close half of the agency's regional offices, and create a new "Administration for a Healthy America."
On April 1, 2025, HHS sent termination notices to 10,000 employees, placing them on administrative leave with formal terminations scheduled for June 2, 2025.

Secretary Kennedy publicly acknowledged that approximately 20% of the layoffs would likely be "mistakes" but stated that conducting a careful line-by-line review would "take too long" and result in lost "political momentum."
The plaintiff states brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging the March 27 Communiqué was both arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.

They also raised constitutional claims for violations of the Separation of Powers doctrine and the Appropriations Clause, arguing that the executive branch lacked authority to effectively dismantle congressionally-created agencies and programs.
The states sought declaratory and injunctive relief to halt the implementation of the reorganization plan.

On May 9, 2025, the states filed a motion for preliminary injunction targeting specific agencies: the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, FDA's Center for Tobacco Products, the Office of Head Start, and the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation.

The states argued they would suffer irreparable harm through loss of critical public health services, laboratory testing capabilities, maternal health data collection, occupational safety programs, tobacco prevention efforts, and federal poverty guideline calculations that their programs and millions of residents depend upon.
Following a hearing on May 20, 2025, Judge DuBose granted the preliminary injunction on July 1, 2025.

The court found that the states had demonstrated a likelihood of success on their APA claims, concluding that the March 27 Communiqué constituted final agency action that was both arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.
The court determined that HHS failed to provide a reasoned explanation for its actions and that the reorganization would prevent the agency from fulfilling numerous congressional mandates.
The court also found the states faced irreparable harm from the disruption of critical public health functions and that the balance of equities favored granting relief.
The court imposed a nominal bond of $100 and denied defendants' request for a stay pending appeal.
On August 12, 2025, defendants filed a notice of appeal to the First Circuit Court of Appeals.

The case involves ongoing disputes over the scope of the preliminary injunction, with the court issuing clarifications on August 12, 2025, specifying that the injunction applies to particular HHS components including CDC divisions, the Center for Tobacco Products, Head Start offices, and the division responsible for federal poverty guidelines.

evidence: Twenty-four states and the District of Columbia filed suit on April 29, 2025, against the Corporation for National and Community Service (operating as AmeriCorps) and its Interim Agency Head Jennifer Bastress Tahmasebi, represented by their respective state attorneys general.
The lawsuit challenges the Trump Administration's dismantling of AmeriCorps, the federal agency for national service and volunteerism that has operated since 1993.

AmeriCorps supports over 200,000 members and volunteers annually through programs like AmeriCorps State and National, the National Civilian Community Corps (NCCC), and Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA).
Beginning in April 2025, the Administration made sweeping cuts to AmeriCorps.
On April 15, AmeriCorps placed all NCCC members—over 750 volunteers engaged in disaster relief and community service—on administrative leave pending termination by April 30.
The next day, AmeriCorps placed 85% of its approximately 720-person staff on administrative leave, reducing the workforce to just 116 employees.
On April 24, AmeriCorps began issuing reduction in force notices.

On April 25, AmeriCorps terminated over 1,000 grants representing nearly $400 million in funding (about half of AmeriCorps' budget), forcing the immediate closure of programs and exit of roughly 32,465 AmeriCorps members, VISTA members, and volunteers nationwide.
The states brought five claims under the Administrative Procedure Act and constitutional law.
They alleged AmeriCorps violated the APA by acting contrary to law, without observing required procedures, and arbitrarily and capriciously.
They also raised a constitutional separation of powers claim and an ultra vires claim.

The central legal issue was AmeriCorps' failure to comply with a statutory requirement in the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, § 401, mandating that AmeriCorps 'make any significant changes to program requirements, service delivery or policy only through public notice and comment rulemaking.'
The states moved for a preliminary injunction on May 6, 2025.
After expedited briefing, a hearing on May 19, 2025, and supplemental briefing, Judge Boardman issued a memorandum opinion and preliminary injunction order on June 5, 2025.

The court found the states likely to succeed on their claim that AmeriCorps violated the notice‑and‑comment requirement, suffered irreparable harm from program closures and loss of services, and that the balance of equities favored relief.
The preliminary injunction was granted in part and denied in part.
The court ordered defendants to restore terminated AmeriCorps programs in the plaintiff states by reinstating grants and returning willing AmeriCorps and VISTA members to service.
It also required restoration of NCCC members to service and compliance with notice‑and‑comment requirements before making significant changes to service delivery.
However, the court denied relief regarding AmeriCorps staffing reductions, finding the states lacked standing to challenge those actions.
The court set a nominal bond of $100 per plaintiff ($2,500 total).
Following the Supreme Court's June 27, 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA limiting universal injunctions, defendants moved to modify the preliminary injunction.

The court granted the consensual modification on July 10, 2025, narrowing the notice‑and‑comment requirement to apply only to actions that harm the plaintiff states, rather than all AmeriCorps actions nationwide.
The states filed an amended complaint on July 24, 2025, and a second motion for preliminary injunction on August 7, 2025.
The case remains active with ongoing proceedings addressing compliance with the preliminary injunction and additional relief sought by the plaintiff states.

evidence: The lawsuit arose from President Trump's March 14, 2025 Executive Order 14238, titled "Continuing the Reduction of the Federal Bureaucracy," which declared IMLS "unnecessary" and directed that it "shall be eliminated to the maximum extent consistent with applicable law." The order required IMLS to "reduce the performance of their statutory functions and associated personnel to the minimum presence and function required by law." Following the Executive Order, Defendants moved swiftly to dismantle IMLS. On March 20, 2025, Trump installed Keith Sonderling, the Deputy Secretary of Labor, as Acting Director of IMLS, though plaintiffs alleged he lacked the statutory qualifications requiring special competence in library or museum services. By March 31, 2025, virtually all of IMLS's approximately 75 employees were placed on indefinite administrative leave and denied access to agency offices and computer systems. On April 3, 2025, Sonderling terminated all but approximately 12 IMLS staff members and fired all 23 members of the congressionally-mandated National Museum and Library Services Board. Defendants also began canceling IMLS grants, including grants to states that are statutorily required under the Museum and Library Services Act.
On May 1, 2025, Judge Leon issued a temporary restraining order providing narrow injunctive relief that preserved the status quo as of May 1, 2025. The TRO was extended until May 29, 2025.

However, after full briefing, Judge Leon denied the motion for a preliminary injunction on June 6, 2025, finding that plaintiffs had not established a likelihood of success on the merits, primarily due to jurisdictional concerns under the Tucker Act. In his June 6, 2025 Memorandum Opinion, Judge Leon found that plaintiffs' claims were likely contractual in nature because they centered on grant terminations, and such claims belong exclusively in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act rather than in district court.

The plaintiffs alleged these actions violated the constitutional separation of powers doctrine and the Take Care Clause, arguing that only Congress has authority to eliminate a statutorily-created agency. They also brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging the dismantling was arbitrary and capricious and exceeded statutory authority, as well as claims under the Impoundment Control Act and Paperwork Reduction Act. Additionally, they asserted ultra vires and First Amendment claims.

evidence: On June 27, 2025, environmental organizations Friends of the Everglades, Inc. and Center for Biological Diversity filed suit in the Southern District of Florida against federal and state officials challenging the construction of a mass immigration detention facility in the Florida Everglades.

The defendants include Kristi Noem (Secretary of Homeland Security), Todd Lyons (Acting Director of ICE), Kevin Guthrie (Executive Director of Florida Division of Emergency Management), and Miami-Dade County.
The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida later intervened as plaintiffs on July 30, 2025.

The case arose after Florida's Division of Emergency Management took control of the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport (TNT) on June 23, 2025, pursuant to a state emergency declaration regarding illegal immigration.
The state rapidly constructed a detention facility dubbed 'Alligator Alcatraz' capable of housing up to 5,000 immigration detainees.

The facility is located within the Big Cypress National Preserve and Big Cypress Area, an environmentally sensitive region that serves as habitat for endangered and threatened species including the Florida panther, Florida bonneted bat, and wood stork.
The facility operates under section 287(g) agreements between ICE and Florida law enforcement agencies, which allow state officers to perform federal immigration functions under federal supervision.

Plaintiffs brought claims under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), alleging that defendants violated NEPA by constructing and operating the facility without preparing an environmental impact statement or environmental assessment.
They also raised state law claims challenging the Florida Division of Emergency Management's authority to operate the facility and Miami-Dade County's acquiescence in the project.
The plaintiffs sought declaratory judgment that defendants' actions violated NEPA and injunctive relief to halt construction and operation until NEPA compliance.
The court conducted an evidentiary hearing on the preliminary injunction motion over four days: August 6, 7, 12, and 13, 2025.
During this hearing, plaintiffs presented testimony from ten witnesses, including environmental experts, organizational representatives, and members who use the Everglades area for recreation.
The testimony focused on potential environmental harms from the facility, including impacts to endangered species habitat, water quality, and the broader Everglades ecosystem.
Defendants presented one witness, the Executive Director of Florida Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, who testified about the facility's operations under 287(g) agreements.

On August 7, 2025, midway through the evidentiary hearing, the court granted plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order, prohibiting defendants from installing additional lighting, paving, filling, excavating, fencing, or expanding the site for fourteen days.
On August 21, 2025, Judge Williams issued an omnibus order granting the preliminary injunction in part and denying it in part.

The court found that venue was proper in the Southern District, rejected defendants' arguments that immigration statutes stripped the court of jurisdiction, determined that NEPA applied to the project as a major federal action, and concluded that plaintiffs demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable harm.

The preliminary injunction ordered defendants to immediately cease transporting new detainees to the facility, immediately cease new construction, and remove all new lighting, fencing, generators, and waste receptacles within sixty days—effectively requiring closure of the facility.
The court required plaintiffs to post only a $100 bond.

Both state and federal defendants have filed appeals and motions to stay the preliminary injunction pending appeal, arguing that the court lacked venue, that NEPA does not apply to state-built facilities, and that the balance of harms favors allowing continued operation of the detention facility.
The case was initially assigned to Judge Jose E. Martinez, who recused on July 16, 2025, and it was reassigned to Judge Kathleen M. Williams.

After defendants challenged venue in the Southern District of Florida, arguing the facility is located in the Middle District, the court held a hearing on venue issues on July 30, 2025, ultimately finding venue proper in the Southern District.

evidence: The case was filed on April 11, 2025, by three organizations—the American Association of University Professors–Harvard Faculty Chapter, the American Association of University Professors, and the International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America—against multiple federal agencies and officials.
The plaintiffs are represented by private counsel from Selendy Gay PLLC and Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll PLLC, and the case is assigned to Judge Allison D. Burroughs.

The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration's systematic campaign to coerce Harvard University into implementing sweeping changes to its operations by threatening and ultimately terminating billions in federal funding.

Beginning in early 2025, the administration launched what it characterized as civil rights enforcement under Title VI, but plaintiffs allege was actually an effort to suppress academic freedom and punish disfavored viewpoints on campus.

On March 31, defendants announced a "comprehensive review" of Harvard's federal funding, encompassing $255.6 million in current grants and $8.7 billion in multi-year commitments, based on alleged failures to address antisemitism.

On April 3, defendants sent Harvard a letter containing nine demands as preconditions for continued funding, including shuttering all diversity, equity, and inclusion programs; implementing merit-based admissions and hiring policies; enacting a comprehensive mask ban; and overhauling student discipline procedures.

An even more extreme letter followed on April 11, demanding governance reforms, mandatory viewpoint diversity audits, faculty reviews for plagiarism, and cooperation with federal authorities on immigration matters.
When Harvard rejected these demands on April 14, 2025, defendants immediately announced a freeze of $2.2 billion in federal funding.
On May 5, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon declared Harvard categorically ineligible for future federal grants.

Between May 6-12, individual agencies sent termination letters ending Harvard's grants, ultimately canceling roughly $2.7 billion in federal funding across multiple agencies including NIH, NSF, DOD, DOE, and others.

Plaintiffs assert two primary legal theories. First, they claim defendants violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to follow the mandatory procedures established by Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for investigating and terminating federal funding based on civil rights violations. These procedures require specific findings, opportunities for voluntary compliance, hearings, and congressional notification—none of which occurred here.

Second, they argue defendants violated the First Amendment through unconstitutional coercion and viewpoint discrimination, using federal funding as leverage to force Harvard to suppress certain academic viewpoints and reshape the university according to the administration's political preferences.

Many faculty members and graduate students represented by the plaintiff organizations have lost their federal funding, forcing them to halt research projects, lay off staff, and abandon ongoing studies.
The funding cuts particularly affected Harvard's School of Public Health, where 60% of the operating budget comes from federal grants.
Plaintiffs filed their motion for summary judgment on June 2, 2025, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief to declare defendants' actions unlawful and restore the terminated funding.
Defendants filed a cross-motion for summary judgment on June 16, 2025.
Oral argument is scheduled for July 21, 2025.
The court has established an expedited briefing schedule given the ongoing harm to research activities and the academic calendar.
This case represents a significant test of the limits of federal power over university operations and the intersection of civil rights enforcement with academic freedom protections.

evidence: On April 11, 2025, the law firm Susman Godfrey LLP filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia challenging Executive Order 14,263, titled "Addressing Risks from Susman Godfrey," which President Trump had issued two days earlier.
The case was assigned to Judge Loren L. AliKhan.

Susman Godfrey, represented by private counsel from Munger, Tolles & Olson LLP, sued numerous federal agencies and officials in their official capacities, seeking declaratory and permanent injunctive relief.
The Executive Order was part of a broader campaign by President Trump targeting law firms that had represented clients or causes he opposed.

The order specifically targeted Susman Godfrey based on the firm's representation of Dominion Voting Systems and state election officials in litigation defending the integrity of the 2020 presidential election, as well as the firm's diversity initiatives and donations to LGBTQ advocacy organizations.

Section 1 of the order accused Susman Godfrey of "spearhead[ing] efforts to weaponize the American legal system and degrade the quality of American elections" and engaging in activities "detrimental to critical American interests."

The order imposed several punitive measures: Section 2 directed immediate suspension of security clearances held by Susman employees; Section 3 required government contractors to disclose business relationships with Susman and directed agencies to terminate contracts involving the firm; Section 4 referenced investigations into the firm's employment practices; and Section 5 restricted Susman employees' access to federal buildings and limited federal employees from engaging with the firm.

Susman Godfrey brought ten constitutional claims, alleging violations of the First Amendment (retaliation for protected speech, viewpoint discrimination, interference with petition rights, and restrictions on freedom of association), the Fifth Amendment (due process violations, vagueness, equal protection violations, and interference with clients' right to counsel), and separation of powers principles.
On April 14, 2025, Susman moved for a temporary restraining order.
Following a hearing on April 15, 2025, Judge AliKhan granted the TRO, temporarily enjoining enforcement of Sections 1, 3, and 5 of the Executive Order.
The court found that the order violated the First and Fifth Amendments and would cause irreparable harm to the firm.
By agreement of the parties, the TRO was extended until final judgment and the case proceeded on an expedited summary judgment schedule.

The case drew significant attention, with twenty-one amicus briefs filed supporting Susman Godfrey from various legal organizations, law professors, former judges, bar associations, and civil rights groups.

Similar executive orders targeting other law firms (Perkins Coie, Jenner & Block, and WilmerHale) were challenged in parallel cases in the same district, with each court finding constitutional violations and issuing permanent injunctions.
On April 23, 2025, Susman moved for summary judgment while defendants moved to dismiss.

Following a hearing on May 8, 2025, Judge AliKhan issued a comprehensive memorandum opinion on June 27, 2025, granting summary judgment in favor of Susman Godfrey on nine of its ten constitutional claims.

The court found that the Executive Order was issued in retaliation for Susman's protected First Amendment activities, constituted impermissible viewpoint discrimination, violated due process by depriving the firm of protected interests without notice or hearing, and exceeded presidential authority in violation of separation of powers principles.

The court permanently enjoined all defendants from implementing or enforcing Executive Order 14,263 in any way, declared the order unconstitutional and null and void, and directed the Department of Justice to notify all affected agencies and personnel of the court's ruling.

The final order represented a complete victory for Susman Godfrey and established important precedent protecting law firms from executive retaliation based on their client representations and advocacy activities.

The order, part of a broader campaign against law firms, imposed punitive measures including suspension of security clearances, disclosure requirements for contractors, termination of contracts, investigations into employment practices, and restrictions on federal building access. Susman Godfrey brought ten constitutional claims alleging First Amendment retaliation, viewpoint discrimination, interference with petition rights, restrictions on freedom of association, Fifth Amendment due process, vagueness, equal protection, interference with clients' right to counsel, and separation of powers violations. A temporary restraining order was granted on April 15, 2025, enjoining Sections 1, 3, and 5; the case drew 21 amicus briefs and similar orders against other law firms were challenged. On June 27, 2025, the court granted summary judgment in favor of Susman on nine of ten claims, permanently enjoining enforcement of the order, declaring it unconstitutional, and directing the Department of Justice to notify agencies. On March 14, 2025, the White House Presidential Personnel Office sent emails terminating all appointed board members without citing any of the statutory grounds for removal.

On March 17, 2025, DOGE personnel forcibly took control of USIP's headquarters building with assistance from law enforcement officers from multiple agencies.

Over the following weeks, the new leadership fired nearly all of USIP's employees, transferred the organization's headquarters building to the General Services Administration without compensation, and moved funds from USIP's private bank accounts to the Treasury, effectively shuttering most operations.
USIP is an independent nonprofit corporation established by Congress in 1984 to promote international peace through research, education, and conflict resolution activities.
